newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts see better outlook for Eridania.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see better outlook for Eridania.

text.p: With the 1996 results of agro-food giant Eridania Beghin-Say unlikely to yield surprises, analysts said they were focusing on prospects for profit growth this year.
Cheaper raw farm material prices are expected to help profit recovery in 1997 though sugar in Italy and starch in the United States remained trouble spots, they said.
Eridania will release its 1996 results on April 3.

It has already said its operating profit for 1996 would drop by some six percent to 3.75 billion francs because some of its businesses suffered from poor 1995 harvests that drove up the prices of raw materials.
The 1996 results should see a rise in net profit because of a stability of financial costs and taxes and a reduction of net exceptional charge.
Dominique Bastien of French brokerage Jean-Pierre Pinatton targets a net attributable profit of 1.565 billion francs for 1996 and of 1.615 billion for 1997 against 1.526 billion in 1995.
Cholet Dupont analyst Annie Bonal expects the net profit to rise to 1.535 billion francs in 1996 and to 1.625 billion francs in 1997.

Analysts warned that profit forecasts mostly hinged on the corporate tax rate applied. They explained that in 1996 Eridania benefited from tax savings linked to the restructuring of its Spanish operations.
They said that a higher tax rate would apply in 1997 unless Eridania carried out a similar restructuring operation, possibly in Germany.
Both analysts predict operating profit may rise to 4.2 billion francs in 1997, helped by lower grain and olive prices resulting from good 1996 harvests.

Oilseeds crushings and refining operations are also expected to benefit from a linkup up with the Bunge group in Spain while the starch sector in Europe will benefit from lower maize and wheat prices.
Analysts also predict a rebound in olive oil consumption in Spain and Italy on the back of cheaper olive prices.
But a poor sugar harvest in Italy and overcapacity plaguing the US starch and sweeteners industry may limit 1997 earning s growth.
"The main unknown involves the negotiation of fructose contracts in the United States," Bonal said.

She was referring to the outcome of price negotiations between suppliers of corn-based fructose syrup and U.S. soft drink companies that started in early 1997. Eridania's Cerestar USA unit is a big player in the U.S. sweeteners market.
Cheaper maize prices should benefit sweeteners producers but extra industry capacity has limited their bargaining power with large soft drink companies.
Analysts said they hoped Eridania's management would provide details on the price negotiations at a results conference scheduled for April 4.
